5.4.4 Hot Spot and Cold Spot Analysis (HCSA) Summary

Weekday AM (6–9 AM)
Hot spots are strongly concentrated in Orchard–Novena, Woodlands–Yishun, Tampines–Bedok, and Jurong East, reflecting intense commuter flows from residential to employment areas. Cold spots occur mainly along Tuas, northern fringes, and green buffer zones, indicating low activity.
Weekday PM (5–8 PM)
Hot spots become fewer and more scattered, with smaller clusters around Tampines, Woodlands, and western interchanges. Cold spots expand across the West and North, showing dispersed evening travel and less concentrated demand.
Weekend / Public Holiday (11 AM–8 PM)
Hot spots reappear at Downtown Core, Tampines, HarbourFront–Sentosa, and Jurong East, driven by leisure and retail trips. Cold spots remain stable in industrial and low-density zones.
Overall, AM peaks show the strongest clustering (commuting), PM peaks are more dispersed, and weekends reflect leisure-oriented movement.



5.4.5 Implication for Transport Planning:

AM peak requires targeted capacity allocation on routes serving residential → employment corridors
PM peak may benefit from more flexible or demand-responsive services.
Weekend planning should emphasize connectivity to leisure and retail destinations rather than traditional commute hubs.
Persistent cold spots can be used to optimize route coverage or evaluate the feasibility of alternative services.

Emerging Hot Spots Analysis (EHSA) is a spatio-temporal statistical technique that identifies and categorizes areas where clusters of high or low values of a phenomenon are developing, intensifying, or diminishing over time.

6.0.1 7.1 Create Space-Time Cubes

# Create monthly aggregated data for EHSA
monthly_trips <- trips_with_month %>%
  group_by(MONTH, MONTH_NUM, HEX_ID, DAY_TYPE) %>%
  summarise(
    AM_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS[HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(6,7,8,9) & DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY"], na.rm = TRUE),
    PM_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS[HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(17,18,19,20) & DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY"], na.rm = TRUE),
    WKD_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS[HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(11:20) & DAY_TYPE == "WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY"], na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Create space-time cubes for each time period
create_spacetime_cube <- function(time_period) {
  cube_data <- monthly_trips %>%
    select(MONTH, MONTH_NUM, HEX_ID, !!sym(time_period)) %>%
    rename(trips = !!sym(time_period)) %>%
    filter(trips > 0) %>%  # Remove zeros for better analysis
    arrange(HEX_ID, MONTH_NUM)
  
  # Join with hexagon geometry
  cube_sf <- hexagon_all %>%
    select(HEX_ID, geometry) %>%
    inner_join(cube_data, by = "HEX_ID")
  
  return(cube_sf)
}

# Create cubes for each period
am_cube <- create_spacetime_cube("AM_TRIPS")
pm_cube <- create_spacetime_cube("PM_TRIPS")

6.0.2 7.2 Calculate Gi* Statistics Over Time

# Function to calculate Gi* for each time slice - FIXED
calculate_gistar_timeseries <- function(cube_data) {
  
  # Get unique months
  months <- unique(cube_data$MONTH_NUM)
  
  results <- list()
  
  for(month_idx in seq_along(months)) {
    current_month <- months[month_idx]
    
    # Filter data for current month and drop geometry for joining
    month_data <- cube_data %>% 
      filter(MONTH_NUM == current_month) %>%
      st_drop_geometry() %>%
      select(HEX_ID, trips)
    
    # Start with hexagon geometry
    complete_data <- hexagon_all %>%
      select(HEX_ID, geometry) %>%
      # Join with month data, filling missing with 0
      left_join(month_data, by = "HEX_ID") %>%
      mutate(trips = replace_na(trips, 0))
    
    # Calculate Gi* for this month
    month_gistar <- complete_data %>%
      mutate(
        nb = st_contiguity(geometry),
        wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W", allow_zero = TRUE),
        gistar = local_gstar_perm(trips, nb, wt, nsim = 99)
      ) %>%
      unnest(gistar) %>%
      mutate(MONTH_NUM = current_month)
    
    results[[as.character(month_idx)]] <- month_gistar
  }
  
  # Combine all months
  final_result <- bind_rows(results)
  return(final_result)
}

6.0.3 7.3 Perform EHSA Analysis

# Perform simplified EHSA for 2 months
perform_ehsa_simple <- function(gistar_ts) {
  
  # Calculate change between months
  ehsa_results <- gistar_ts %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(HEX_ID, MONTH_NUM, gi_star, p_sim, cluster) %>%
    group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
    arrange(MONTH_NUM) %>%
    summarise(
      month1_gi = first(gi_star),
      month2_gi = last(gi_star),
      month1_sig = first(p_sim < 0.05),
      month2_sig = last(p_sim < 0.05),
      month1_cluster = first(cluster),
      month2_cluster = last(cluster),
      gi_change = month2_gi - month1_gi,
      .groups = 'drop'
    ) %>%
    # Classify based on 2-month pattern
    mutate(
      ehsa_category = case_when(
        # Intensifying: Was hot spot and becoming stronger
        month1_sig & month2_sig & month1_cluster == "High" & month2_cluster == "High" & gi_change > 0 ~ "Intensifying",
        # Emerging: Was not significant, now hot spot
        !month1_sig & month2_sig & month2_cluster == "High" ~ "Emerging",
        # Diminishing: Was hot spot, now weaker or not significant
        month1_sig & month1_cluster == "High" & (!month2_sig | gi_change < 0) ~ "Diminishing",
        # Persistent: Stable hot spot
        month1_sig & month2_sig & month1_cluster == "High" & month2_cluster == "High" & abs(gi_change) < 0.5 ~ "Persistent",
        # Sporadic: Inconsistent pattern
        month1_sig != month2_sig ~ "Sporadic",
        # Cold spot patterns (similar logic but for low clusters)
        month1_sig & month2_sig & month1_cluster == "Low" & month2_cluster == "Low" & gi_change < 0 ~ "Intensifying Cold",
        !month1_sig & month2_sig & month2_cluster == "Low" ~ "Emerging Cold",
        month1_sig & month1_cluster == "Low" & (!month2_sig | gi_change > 0) ~ "Diminishing Cold",
        month1_sig & month2_sig & month1_cluster == "Low" & month2_cluster == "Low" & abs(gi_change) < 0.5 ~ "Persistent Cold",
        TRUE ~ "No Clear Pattern"
      )
    )
  
  return(ehsa_results)
}

# Plot time series for selected hexagons with interesting patterns
interesting_categories <- c("Intensifying", "Emerging", "Diminishing")
interesting_hexagons <- am_ehsa %>%
  filter(ehsa_category %in% interesting_categories) %>%
  pull(HEX_ID)

# If we have interesting patterns, plot them
if(length(interesting_hexagons) > 0) {
  
  # Select top 6 for visualization
  plot_hexagons <- head(interesting_hexagons, 6)
  
  # Prepare plot data
  trend_plot_data <- am_gistar_ts %>%
    filter(HEX_ID %in% plot_hexagons) %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(HEX_ID, MONTH_NUM, gi_star, p_sim, cluster) %>%
    left_join(am_ehsa %>% select(HEX_ID, ehsa_category), by = "HEX_ID") %>%
    mutate(
      Month = case_when(
        MONTH_NUM == 1 ~ "August",
        MONTH_NUM == 2 ~ "September"
      ),
      Month = factor(Month, levels = c("August", "September")),
      significant = p_sim < 0.05
    )
  
  # Create trend plot
  trend_plot <- ggplot(trend_plot_data, aes(x = Month, y = gi_star, group = HEX_ID, color = ehsa_category)) +
    geom_line(size = 1.2) +
    geom_point(aes(shape = significant), size = 3) +
    geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(significant, cluster, "")), 
              vjust = -1, size = 3, color = "black") +
    facet_wrap(~HEX_ID, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
    labs(
      title = "Gi* Statistic Trends for Selected Hexagons (AM Peak)",
      subtitle = "Labels show cluster type (High/Low) when statistically significant (p < 0.05)",
      x = "Month",
      y = "Gi* Statistic",
      color = "EHSA Category",
      shape = "Statistically\nSignificant"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("Intensifying" = "red", 
                                 "Emerging" = "orange",
                                 "Diminishing" = "blue")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c("TRUE" = 16, "FALSE" = 1)) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey80"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "lightblue", color = "grey50")
    )
  
  print(trend_plot)
  
} else {
  cat("No intensifying, emerging, or diminishing patterns to plot.\n")
}

title: Take_Home Ex02: Singapore Bus Mobility and Urban Development Patterns
text:
7 8. Conclusion
This analysis of Singapore’s bus network reveals a system characterized by strong, organized spatial patterns rather than random passenger distribution. The methodological approach, progressing from basic mapping to advanced statistical clustering, provides a clear and evidence-based understanding of urban mobility.
Key Findings from the Analytical Process:

Spatial Distribution Analysis (Hexagon Mapping): The initial aggregation of bus stops into hexagonal zones provided a clear visual foundation. It immediately revealed that passenger demand is not uniform but concentrates in specific, identifiable areas across the island.
Spatial Autocorrelation (Global and Local Moran’s I): Statistical testing confirmed that the observed clustering is significant and not random. The fact that areas of high demand are surrounded by other high-demand areas (and likewise for low-demand areas) confirms that passenger movements follow predictable spatial structures.
Hot Spot Analysis (Getis-Ord Gi*): This technique successfully pinpointed the exact locations of statistically significant hotspots and cold spots. The alignment of these zones with known urban centers and transport nodes validates the current network design while highlighting areas of unexpected high or low usage.
Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA): By incorporating the time dimension, the study demonstrated how these clusters are evolving. The identification of “Intensifying,” “Emerging,” and “Diminishing” areas provides a dynamic view of demand shifts, crucial for forward-looking planning.

Interpretation and Strategic Implications:
The findings indicate that Singapore’s bus network efficiently serves a spatially structured demand pattern. The clear distinction between weekday commute corridors and weekend leisure destinations underscores a successful alignment with the city’s land-use patterns.
From a planning perspective, the consistent identification of key clusters across multiple analytical methods offers a robust evidence base for decision-making. This enables a shift from reactive service adjustments to a more proactive and strategic approach. Resources can be prioritized with greater confidence, targeting investments and service enhancements toward zones of growing demand, while optimizing or re-allocating resources from areas of declining use.
In conclusion, this multi-layered analytical framework transforms complex mobility data into actionable intelligence. It provides a reliable foundation for ensuring that Singapore’s bus network continues to evolve in step with the changing needs of its population, enhancing both efficiency and service quality.

title: In-class Ex08: Take-home Exercise 3 Kick Starter
text:
Data Wrangling
The HDB resale data can be downloaded from here. The dataset contains resale flat prices based on registration date from Jan 2017 to Sep 2024.
The code below reads the raw CSV file containing the resale flat data and filters it to include only records from January 2023 to September 2024.

resale <- read_csv("data/ResaleflatpricesbasedonregistrationdatefromJan2017onwards.csv") %>%
  filter(flat_type=="4 ROOM") %>%
  filter(month >= "2025-09" & month <= "2025-10")

The following code tidies the data by creating new columns: - address: Combines block and street_name to form a complete address. - remaining_lease_yr: Extracts the remaining lease years as an integer. - remaining_lease_mth: Extracts the remaining lease months as an integer.

resale_tidy <- resale %>%
  mutate(address = paste(block,street_name)) %>%
  mutate(remaining_lease_yr = as.integer(
    str_sub(remaining_lease, 0, 2)))%>%
  mutate(remaining_lease_mth = as.integer(
    str_sub(remaining_lease, 9, 11)))

Next, we filter the tidy dataset to include only records from September 2024.

resale_selected <- resale_tidy %>%
  filter(month == "2024-09")

Then, we generate a sorted list of unique addresses from the filtered dataset. This will be used to retrieve geographical coordinates.

add_list <- sort(unique(resale_selected$address))

In the code below, the get_coords function retrieves latitude and longitude coordinates for each address in the list. It uses the OneMap API to query addresses and returns a dataframe with postal codes and geographical coordinates: - If a single result is found, the coordinates are retrieved and stored. - If multiple results are found, addresses with “NIL” as postal are dropped, and the top result is selected. - If no valid results are found, NA is stored.

get_coords <- function(add_list){

  # Create a data frame to store all retrieved coordinates
  postal_coords <- data.frame()

  for (i in add_list){
    #print(i)

    r <- GET('https://www.onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search?',
           query=list(searchVal=i,
                     returnGeom='Y',
                     getAddrDetails='Y'))
    data <- fromJSON(rawToChar(r$content))
    found <- data$found
    res <- data$results

    # Create a new data frame for each address
    new_row <- data.frame()

    # If single result, append
    if (found == 1){
      postal <- res$POSTAL
      lat <- res$LATITUDE
      lng <- res$LONGITUDE
      new_row <- data.frame(address= i,
                            postal = postal,
                            latitude = lat,
                            longitude = lng)
    }

    # If multiple results, drop NIL and append top 1
    else if (found > 1){
      # Remove those with NIL as postal
      res_sub <- res[res$POSTAL != "NIL", ]

      # Set as NA first if no Postal
      if (nrow(res_sub) == 0) {
          new_row <- data.frame(address= i,
                                postal = NA,
                                latitude = NA,
                                longitude = NA)
      }

      else{
        top1 <- head(res_sub, n = 1)
        postal <- top1$POSTAL
        lat <- top1$LATITUDE
        lng <- top1$LONGITUDE
        new_row <- data.frame(address= i,
                              postal = postal,
                              latitude = lat,
                              longitude = lng)
      }
    }

    else {
      new_row <- data.frame(address= i,
                            postal = NA,
                            latitude = NA,
                            longitude = NA)
    }

    # Add the row
    postal_coords <- rbind(postal_coords, new_row)
  }
  return(postal_coords)
}

We apply the function to the list of addresses and the retrieved coordinates are saved as an RDS file for future use.

coords <- get_coords(add_list)

write_rds(coords, "data/model/mdata.rds")

This concludes the sample exercise on how to handle the dataset for Take-Home Exercise 3B.

We will proceed with In-Class Exercise 08 next.

Checking of overlapping point






Warning



When using GWmodel to calibrate explanatory or predictive models, it is very important to ensure that there are no overlapping point features.


The code block below is used to check if there are overlapping point features.

overlapping_points <- HDB_sample %>%
  mutate(overlap = lengths(st_equals(., .)) > 1)


Spatial jitter
In the code code block below, st_jitter() of sf package is used to move the point features by 5m to avoid overlapping point features.

HDB_sample <- HDB_sample %>%
  st_jitter(amount = 5)

text:
Train-Test Split
Note that in this case, we use random sampling method to split the data into training and testing sets. No stratification was applied. (We should adopt a stratification method for Take-Home Exercise 3B to ensure better representation across subgroups.)
We will use initial_split() of rsample package. rsample is a package from tidymodels framework.

set.seed(1234)
resale_split <- initial_split(mdata,
                              prop = 6.67/10,)
train_data <- training(resale_split)
test_data <- testing(resale_split)


write_rds(train_data, "data/model/train_data.rds")
write_rds(test_data, "data/model/test_data.rds")


train_data <- read_rds("data/model/train_data.rds")
test_data <- read_rds("data/model/test_data.rds")


Multicolinearity Check
Multicollinearity can affect the stability and interpretability of a regression model. To identify potential multicollinearity, we will use ggcorrmat() of ggstatsplot to plot a correlation matrix to check if there are pairs of highly correlated independent variables.

mdata_nogeo <- mdata %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(mdata_nogeo[, 2:17]) #columns 2 to 17 to plot Correlation Matrix

Building Non-Spatial Multiple Linear Regression
When constructing predictive models, it is advisable to avoid including all variables to avoid overfitting. Instead, only the most relevant predictors that contribute to the model’s performance should be selected.
On the other hand, explanatory models aim to understand relationships between variables and identify which factors have significant effects on the outcome. In such cases, including all variables can help provide a clearer picture of these relationships.

                  storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +

text:
Predictive Modelling with gwr

Computing Adaptive Bandwidth
An adaptive bandwidth is calculated using geographically weighted regression (GWR), which allows for local variations in relationships between variables.

# Compute adaptive bandwidth
bw_adaptive <- bw.gwr(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
                  storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
                  PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
                  PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL +
                  PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
                  WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
                  WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
                  data=train_data,
                  approach="CV",
                  kernel="gaussian",
                  adaptive=TRUE,
                  longlat=FALSE)

Then, we save this model for future use:

# Save adaptive bandwidth
write_rds(bw_adaptive, "data/model/bw_adaptive.rds")


bw_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/bw_adaptive.rds")



Model Calibration
The GWR model is then calibrated to examine spatially varying relationships:

# Calibrate gwr-based hedonic pricing model
gwr_adaptive <- gwr.basic(formula = resale_price ~
                            floor_area_sqm + storey_order +
                            remaining_lease_mths + PROX_CBD +
                            PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
                            PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL +
                            PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
                            WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
                            WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
                          data=train_data,
                          bw = bw_adaptive,
                          kernel = 'gaussian',
                          adaptive=TRUE,
                          longlat = FALSE)

Then, we save this calibrated model for future use:

# Save calibrated model
write_rds(gwr_adaptive, "data/model/gwr_adaptive.rds")


gwr_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/gwr_adaptive.rds")



Predicting with test data

# Compute test data adaptive bandwidth
gwr_bw_test_adaptive <- bw.gwr(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
                  storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
                  PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
                  PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL +
                  PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
                  WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
                  WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
                  data=test_data,
                  approach="CV",
                  kernel="gaussian",
                  adaptive=TRUE,
                  longlat=FALSE)

Then, we save the output for future use:

write_rds(gwr_bw_test_adaptive,
          "data/model/gwr_bw_test.rds")


# #| eval: False
gwr_bw_test_adaptive <- read_rds(
  "data/model/gwr_bw_test.rds")

To compute the predicted values:

# Compute predicted values
gwr_pred <- gwr.predict(formula = resale_price ~
                          floor_area_sqm + storey_order +
                          remaining_lease_mths + PROX_CBD + 
                          PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + 
                          PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL + 
                          PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
                          WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +

                        data=train_data, 
                        predictdata = test_data, 
                        bw=bw_adaptive,

                        adaptive=TRUE,

gwRF_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/gwRF_adaptive.rds")







Tip



The global model is a ranger object which can provide additional insights:

Local Variable Importance: This metric calculates the importance of each variable for every data point, allowing us to see which predictors are more influential in different locations.
Local Goodness of Fit (LGofFit): For each data point, the model assesses how well the local predictions match the observed values, offering insights into model performance across different areas.
Forests: Each local forest contains various metrics, such as sample size, to understand the local behavior and conditions affecting predictions.





Predict with Test Data
Since the GRF model requires coordinate data as part of its input, the coordinates from the test data need to be merged with the original dataset after removing the geometry field.

test_data_nogeom <- cbind(
  test_data, coords_test) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

Next, predict.grf() of spatialML package will be used to predict the resale value by using the test data and gwRF_adaptive model calibrated earlier.

gwRF_pred <- predict.grf(gwRF_adaptive,
                         test_data_nogeom,
                         x.var.name="X",
                         y.var.name="Y",
                         local.w=1,
                         global.w=0,
                         nthreads = 4)


GRF_pred <- write_rds(gwRF_pred, "data/model/GRF_pred.rds")


GRF_pred <- read_rds("data/model/GRF_pred.rds")
# create df
GRF_pred_df <- as.data.frame(GRF_pred)

To analyze the differences between the predicted and actual values, the predictions are merged back with the test dataset to compare predicted against actual resale prices.

# Combine predicted values with test data
test_data_pred <- cbind(test_data, GRF_pred_df)

Save the combined data for future reference:

write_rds(test_data_pred, "data/model/test_data_pred.rds")


test_data_pred <- read_rds("data/model/test_data_pred.rds")

To calculate Root Mean Square Error (RMSE):

rmse(test_data_pred$resale_price,
     test_data_pred$GRF_pred)

[1] 28955.92


To visualize the predicted vs actual value with a scatterplot.

ggplot(data = test_data_pred,
       aes(x = GRF_pred,
           y = resale_price)) +
  geom_point()








Ideally, points should align along the diagonal line, indicating accurate predictions. Points below it show underestimation, while points above indicate overestimation of price prediction.
